# CB RULES for the animator (GENERATED 2026-11-15 by tools/slice_rules.py from CB_RULES.md; do not edit)
CB_RULES.md is the master and wins. This file holds the rules that touch your job. Read it instead of the whole book. If a rule you need seems missing, grep CB_RULES.md for the word; do not read it top to bottom.

## RULE NO. 1: MAKE A RICK-QUALITY VIDEO. If this fails, everything is wrong.
(CB 2026-11-11: "no1 rule is to make ricks quality video", "if is fails everything is wrong")
- [ ] Every rule below serves this one. Following a workflow step, passing a gate or ticking a box never excuses a result that is below Rick's.
- [ ] THE TEST, on every picture and every clip before CB sees it: put ours next to a Rick frame of the same kind of shot (same shot size, same kind of place). Ask plainly: would this pass as a frame from his channel? Look at story clarity, world detail, light and shadow, reflection, colour, acting, camera.
- [ ] If ours is clearly weaker, it is NOT done. Fix it, or tell CB exactly what is still below Rick and why. Never present it as finished.
- [ ] If a workflow, tool or note leads to a result below Rick, the workflow is wrong: stop, say so, and use the method that reached the quality before (the airfield way).

## HARD RULE NO. 2: NOTHING GENERIC PASSES. EVERYTHING IS ULTRA DETAILED. (CB 2026-11-11: "Can we add rules hard rule. Nothing generic wont pass. Everything need to be ultra detailed")
This is a gate, not advice. A frame that fails it is not shown to CB and not rendered further.
- **Generic = fail.** A plain box, ball tree, flat one-colour surface, typed font, filler word, star in place of a word, empty prop, standing or floor-sit pose where the story needs a real action, or a set that could belong to any film.
- **Every object in frame is specific to THIS story** and built from real parts, down to the small things: a wallet has pockets, stitching, a photo and flies that fly out; a board carries a real blueprint; a cart carries the ride's name; a loop under construction shows the crane and the missing piece.
- **Scale is checked:** trees about a quarter of the hero structure, a vehicle small around its rider, characters as large in frame as Rick's.
- **Poses are specific:** seated means a chair-sit with knees forward, sleeping means slumped with a tilt; body moves come from the trained motion library.
- **The test before CB sees it:** put the frame beside Rick's and name five specific details in every main object. If you cannot, or if Rick's shows a kind of thing ours lacks, it fails. Fix it first.
Full detail list: section 3, "PREMIUM DETAIL IN EVERYTHING".

## 11. THE LEAN PIPELINE AND THE TOKEN RULES (CB 2026-11-15 after the armor film: "how we can optimized that is not burn too much tokes and quicker to make", "or what takes so much time and not worth", then "yes please do."). Wins over every older pipeline line in this file and in SKILL.md.
Why: the armor film (63.5 s) cost 1.66 billion tokens, 41 helpers and 22.7 working hours. Measured: about 750 million went into a still-picture storyboard with judge rounds that CB rejected when he saw it move; 97 % of all tokens were re-reading (every step a helper takes re-reads everything it has seen so far); builder 1 alone cost 184 million because one conversation ran 13 hours. Target for the next film of the same quality: at most 450 million tokens and 12 working hours.

### 11a. The lean pipeline (the order of work)
1. STORY AND VOICE, THEN THE PICTURE PLAN. One story unless CB asks for a choice; facts checked; voice recorded; `words.json`; then `PICTURE_PLAN.md` (11d): what the viewer sees on each word, written for this story.
2. THE ONE GATE: THE WHOLE FILM ROUGH, PLUS THE HOOK MOVING. As soon as script, voice and the first character are locked, one builder per stretch starts at once (section 10) with a cap of 60-90 minutes and brings 2-3 real three.js key frames for EVERY line of its stretch: no polish, stand-in cast allowed. The hook builder also brings its 10-15 s in motion with voice and captions. CB sees the picture plan, the whole board with its line check and the moving hook together, and says yes or no. Nothing is polished and no judge runs before this gate. Why both: the armor film showed that stills cannot prove motion or camera (CB rejected what the stills had passed); the Moonrakers film showed that polishing one scene for a day before CB has seen the whole film wastes the day (CB 2026-11-14: "til now i dint see the storybaord", then "Board all 20 lines now"). This replaces the hook-frame gate of section 0.
3. BUILD OUT AND POLISH THE STRETCHES from the approved board, in parallel (section 10), from ONE shared sets folder from the first day (never a copy of the sets per stretch), with the strong colours already in (11c). CB's approved board is the FLOOR: a polished frame keeps every story element its board panel shows (props, characters, the gag, the named thing) and the light of its chapter; the builder checks board beside polish before reporting.
4. CB'S NOTES IN BATCHES. The lead collects all notes on a version, runs the automatic checks first, then sends ONE fix round per version. Aim: two rounds.
5. SOUND, then THE GRADE as the last picture step, then delivery.
ONE FOLDER PER FILM (CB 2026-11-15: "never create so many subfolder. for one keep same name and create inside subfolder with version"). A film lives in ONE folder, `episodes/<name>/`, named after the film, never after a prompt or a task. Stretches, versions, fixes and tests go INSIDE it: `episodes/<name>/s2/`, `episodes/<name>/v3/`, `episodes/<name>/_tmp/`. Never a sibling folder such as `<name>-s2`, `<name>-s4a-raid`, `_ridefix_tmp_s4a` or `continue-<name>-from-handoff...`. Every helper brief names its subfolder inside the film folder. Temp folders are deleted when their stretch lands. At delivery the film folder keeps the final video, the scripts, the notes and the code; frame folders, old versions and logs are deleted. DELETE DIRECTLY, WITHOUT ASKING, as soon as the final is approved (CB 2026-11-15: "next time please delete directly after everything final keep only neccessary files and final files"): keep the final video(s), scripts, notes, code, cast, refs, sets and sound; delete every frame folder, old version, old animatic, log and temp folder. Then decode the kept final once to prove it plays.
Not in the pipeline any more, used only when CB asks for them by name:
- Department rounds on still pictures BEFORE the gate (camera, light, props and effects each sending fix rounds on a storyboard) and judge loops. On the armor film three such rounds chased judge scores of 5.5 and 6.8 and none of that work reached the film; on Moonrakers six judge and fix rounds went into 7.5 s while 18 lines were not started. A judge runs at most ONCE per version, AFTER the gate, on the moving clip and its sheets; never judge, fix, judge more than twice without CB seeing the version. The lead still LOOKS at the check sheets before CB sees anything (section 7 stays).
- A Blender layer. It cost about 80 million tokens and 6 hours for a gain that is hard to see on a phone. Use it only when a polished, glass or wet hero object is the star of the story, test it on 2 frames first, and put it only where that object covers at least 1.5 % of the picture.
- A repaint of finished sets. Colour is decided before the sets are built (11c).

### 11b. Token rules (every helper and the lead)
- T1 READ ONLY YOUR SLICE. A helper reads `rules/dept/<its department>.md` (made by `python tools/slice_rules.py`) and the files its brief names. It never reads the whole of CB_RULES.md or SKILL.md; when it needs one more rule it greps for the word. Only the lead reads the whole book, once per session.
- T2 A FRESH HELPER FOR EVERY FIX ROUND. A helper does one build or one fix round, then it ends. Before it reports it writes `STATE.md` in its work folder (at most 60 lines): what is built, the files and frame folders, the numbers measured, what is weak, what is open. The next round is a NEW helper that reads STATE.md and the notes. Never resume a helper that already did a round: each resumed step re-reads its whole history. (This replaces "one builder who stays through every fix round" in section 10.)
- T3 NUMBERS BEFORE PICTURES. Anything a script can measure is checked by a script that prints numbers: a figure cut by the frame edge, the named thing in frame on its word, floor share, saturation and brightness, frozen frames, loudness. A helper opens a picture only when a number fails or for the one final look. Pictures are looked at small: one sheet at most 1,600 px wide, at most 4 pictures per check round, never full-size frames one by one.
- T4 ONE COMMAND PER CYCLE. Render, sheets and measurements run from ONE script call. A long run goes in the background and the helper ends its turn; it does not wake up to wait, poll or look at a log. Every wake-up re-reads everything.
- T5 SHORT REPORTS, DETAIL IN FILES. A helper's report is at most 25 lines: done, numbers, weak points, files. Tables and lists go into a file the report names.
- T6 THE SMALL MODEL FOR MECHANICAL WORK. Rendering, joining, measuring, merging, fact checks, sound mix runs and file moves go to a helper on the smaller model (Agent tool `model: sonnet` or `haiku`). The main model is for story, acting, camera and look decisions.
- T7 A FRESH LEAD SESSION PER PHASE. Story, build and finish are three sessions, each started from HANDOFF.md. The lead never reads a helper's transcript and never pastes long tool output into the chat when a file path will do.
- T8 NOTHING BUILT TWICE. Before a helper builds a tool, a set part or a move, it greps `tools/`, `templates/` and the last episode for one that exists. Studies of Rick are done once and live in the rules and `references/`; a film does not study him again unless CB names a new question.
- T9 MEASURE EVERY FILM. At delivery the lead runs `python tools/token_report.py` and writes the totals into HANDOFF.md: tokens per helper, working hours, and the three most expensive helpers with the reason. A helper over 60 million tokens is a fault to explain.

### 11c. Colour from the first day
- The LOOK_BIBLE carries the measured targets before any set is built: saturation of the ungraded frames at least 0.36 for the whole film and 0.30 by day, a clearly different colour world per kind of light (distance between light kinds at least 18 before the grade), night frames never under mean brightness 0.31, one red in the film, faces white by day.
- Sets start from the armor film's coloured values (`episodes/armor-no-holes/colour_pass/COLOUR_PASS.md`: the pigment key `rich`, the light colours per place), not from grey defaults.
- The grade is the last picture step and is cheap (armor: 8 million tokens, 3 minutes for the whole film): start from `episodes/armor-no-holes/grade_final/` (per light kind, with the guards for reds, faces, caption letters and the ceiling).

### 11d. Solve it before it is built (CB 2026-11-15: "i want it have the problem solve in first place not to much fine tune", then "every story is different. it need to match to the story")
Why: of CB's 23 notes on the armor film about 14 were "the thing the voice names is not shown, not close enough or not highlighted", about 5 were "someone is cut off or stands wrong", about 4 were acting or a gag. Almost all were knowable before a frame was built.
- THE PICTURE PLAN, BEFORE ANY BUILD. After the script and voice the writer and the lead write `episodes/<name>/PICTURE_PLAN.md` in the format of `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md`: one row for every thing or action the voice names, with the word it lands on, what we see, CLOSE / IN SCENE / NOT SHOWN and WHY in this story, the character's feeling on that word, an effect or gag only if this story's world gives one. CB approves it with the rough board (the one gate). Every row is a must for the builder; the line-check sheet is ordered by its rows.
- THE STORY DECIDES, NEVER A TEMPLATE. The plan is a format, not content: it is written fresh from each script and no row is copied from another film. A close-up goes in only where it fits the scene (section 10: secondary, must match the scene). "The voice says it" is not a reason; the reason is what the thing does in the story. Rick's numbers (96 % shown on the word, about 40 % close) check the total at the end and are never a quota per line.
- A LIBRARY OF PIECES IS TECHNIQUE, NOT CONTENT. Proven pieces live in `templates/pieces/` (built 2026-11-15 from the armor film: 17 pieces; 12 as code = hop, laugh, hit, double tap, live stroke, "got it", "told you so", the motion helpers, highlight of a part, fly-and-hit, burst of living things, time pass; 5 as numbers only = push-in, low-angle close-up, fly through an object, fly-land-rest, the "hundreds" count). Read `templates/pieces/INDEX.md`: each entry says WHEN IT FITS and when not, and what must change. `node templates/pieces/prove.mjs` and `prove_fx.mjs` must print PASS after any edit there. Known limits: the amounts of lean, arm and head inside a move are still the armor characters' and need an animator for another body; effect files give numbers per frame, the look is built new in the film's set module; the first film that imports a piece tests ONE move through the kit first (`templates/pieces/STATE.md`). A plan row names the piece AND what changes for this story (object, light, character). A piece used unchanged is generic and fails Hard Rule No. 2.
- AUTOMATIC FRAME CHECKS BEFORE CB SEES A VERSION: `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs <film.json>` (built and proven 2026-11-15; about 40 s per stretch, quarter size, one process). On every camera rest it tests, per character: head with hat cut by the frame edge; the figure cut through by a side edge; set geometry between the camera and the face, or the head inside a mesh; feet floating or sunk. It prints numbers, saves one small crop per FAIL and exits 1 on a FAIL. Every builder runs it before reporting, and the lead before CB sees a version. A version with a FAIL is not sent, unless the picture-plan row says in words that the figure at the edge is meant (a CLOSE on a thing with a face at the edge); such a waiver is named in the report. Proof: it caught three planted faults (head cut 23 %, body cut 49 %, head inside the engine) and found the Chief's face cut in half at the edge of the chalk close-up in the approved armor film (S1 frames 184-205), which nobody had seen. Limits: three.js stage only, not a Blender pass; one character covering another is not reported; a moving character is exempt on that frame; tuned on two stretches of one film.
- A NOTE FROM CB IS CHECKED AGAINST THE PLAN. Was the row there? If not, the row is added to the film's plan, and if the kind of thing was missing from the format, `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md` gets the line, so the next film's plan catches it.

## 2. Every picture (the mechanism)
- [ ] FRAME 0 IS THE HOOK: a character doing the strange act with the hero object readable. Never an object close-up, at the start or as the loop frame. ("start frame should be something noticeable, a hook")
- [ ] One idea per picture = the words being spoken. Doer + thing + result in the same frame. New phrase = new picture or a clear move.
- [ ] SILENT TEST: the action is acted out, so the story reads with the sound off. ("you understand the work without having the narration tell anything")
- [ ] 2-4 elements, subject big, nothing in front of the subject or the hero object. No empty frames.
- [ ] Literal sense: the picture must make sense for the line and the place. ("why standing sleeping that not make sense")
- [ ] Stay in the story's world: analogy scenes use the same period, place and cast. No modern set in a period story.
- [ ] Exaggerate the idea as a funny prop or scale, not as random effects.

## 5. Movement and acting
- [ ] NEVER A STATIC KIT POSE (CB 2026-11-13 evening, bomber armor animatic: "rules never use static kit pose. we made a rule for movement yesterday night", "no natural body movement, see the fireworks test we did it much better. you forgot something"). The kit's plain poses (stand, hold_out, knock, hold_up, hands_hips, grip_* used as a frozen stance ...) are blocking stand-ins only and never reach a storyboard, an animatic or CB. Every act of every character is a MOVE that plays through time (`m:<id>`): an episode move written for that action, or a trained library move for walks, climbs, kneels and carries (picked by action, feeling, energy and character, with its reason in the shot table), with the way in and the way out acted (walk in, kneel, climb, carry, turn). A prop grip is a library move with the grip on it, never a frozen grip pose. The bomber armor film went to CB with 100 of 103 poses static and not one walk: that is the failure this rule names. GATE (to be built into tools/film_plan.py; until then the lead counts by hand before any storyboard render): fail on any act whose pose is not `m:`, on a frozen move (`@=`), on `walk: true` with the planner's stand-in walk, on a film without `"tween": { "ones": true }`, and on `face_frames` above 0 (faces change as a step). A move the library lacks is designed in three styles and added first.
  CORRECTION (CB 2026-11-13, same evening: "the fireworks test clip. it move from itself. we didnt train it, followed another rule that we made"): natural body movement comes from TWO rules together, and the fireworks test used the second. (1) Trained library moves for the cycles and set pieces (walk, run, climb, kneel, carry ...). (2) STUDIO MOTION for every other action (`cloud_rules/motion/STUDIO_MOTION.md`): the body moves by itself through the action sequence NOTICE, READ, ANTICIPATE, HOLD, STRIKE, IMPACT, REACT, SETTLE, DEAD STILL, on ones, with the snap curve (about 70 % of the move in 5 frames, then a slow settle), the head leading a notice and lagging a strike, hands travelling on arcs, a counter-move before every strike, props and hanging things settling after the hand stops, all solved with BODY MECHANICS (fixed limb lengths, the hand goes to its target and the body follows). A pose change that jumps or blends straight from A to B without that sequence is a static kit pose in disguise and fails the same gate.
- [ ] EVERY ACTION IS A MOVE, DRAWN NEW ON EVERY FRAME (CB 2026-11-13 evening "yes make it as rule"; found in the fireworks test lock, where the boy has 636 drawings for 636 frames and every one belongs to a move: kneel, pocket, flick, light, take, brave, flee, lookup, rise, home). How it is built, for every film: 1 film.json sets `"tween": { "ones": true }`. 2 Each action of each character in the script is written as its own EPISODE MOVE (`m:<name>`, a time-driven move function in the motion-library form, played by the kit's motion-library bridge in `templates/threejs_film/puppets.mjs`), built as a STUDIO MOTION action sequence, so the body animates itself through the whole action. 3 Faces come from `faces_ep` and change on the words INSIDE the move. 4 Hands follow per-frame targets on the real prop anchors (`hand_at`, `held3d`). 5 Walks, climbs, kneels and carries come from the trained library. 6 Small living things (a cat, a bird) get their own short pose sequences. A film whose acts are plain poses is not staged yet. CHECK before any storyboard: per character, drawings per second in the lock or the baked performance (the fireworks boy: 30 a second while he acts; the bomber armor animatic: frozen poses with a 7-frame blend).
- [ ] THE NEWEST MOTION METHOD IN EVERY CLIP, NEVER A TEST MOVE (CB 2026-11-14, goldrush hook clip: "it looks stif. dindt you sue the latest update on motion ?", then "Yes, add the rule"). Why: the lead sent the character-artist's TEST move (gr_hook.mjs, a plain repeating sine run cycle written only to prove the bottle in the hand) to the render brief, so the first hook clip looked stiff; the newest method lived in the newest episode folder, not in this file. Rule: (1) at the start of every film the lead finds the newest motion method: the top section of HANDOFF.md, the newest episode's moves/ folder (2026-11-14: episodes/moonrakers/moves/ ROUND 4, ep_moonrakers.mjs, studio_ep.mjs) and cloud_rules/motion/STUDIO_MOTION.md, and names it in the animator's first brief. (2) Every move in a clip or animatic CB sees is written by the animator in that method (STUDIO MOTION episode moves, drawn new on every frame, timed on words.json) and passes the motion gate before the render: episodes/moonrakers/moves/tools/check_motion_ep.mjs (copied into the film's moves/tools/) = 0 twos, 0 linear, 0 no-settle, 0 creep, contact 0 px, plus plain kit poses 0, frozen moves 0, and no body hold over about 1 s while a character is acting (silhouettes compared on the 4 fps strip). (3) A test move from another department (a pose proof, a hand test) says TEST in its first line and never goes into a render brief. Enforced by: the lead's brief check and the gate numbers written in the clip's check file.
- [ ] HANDS ARE ALWAYS THE ROUND FIST, NEVER A 3D HAND (CB 2026-11-14, goldrush hook v7 close-up: "also the hand always is a round hand. dont generate the hand in 3d."). Every character's hand in every shot, close-ups included, is the cast's round fist drawn by the kit, sitting ON the object. No 3D glove, no realHand with fingers, no hand model. This REPLACES the SKILL.md line "Close-ups use realHand, a glove with wrapped fingers". If a close-up reads badly (the fist merges with a dark part of the prop), fix the framing, the light or the prop, never the hand.
- [ ] LESSONS LIVE IN THIS FILE (CB 2026-11-13: "everything we learnd from there should be here already. i dont know why it didnt update here"). Why it happened: the lessons of the cloud threads (studio motion, fireworks test, roller coaster, cart army) were copied to the PC only as side notes under `cloud_rules/` and `memory/`, with a README saying they replace nothing, and were never merged into CB_RULES.md; the lead of the bomber armor film read CB_RULES, SKILL and HANDOFF and never opened them. From now on: a lesson is finished only when its rule text is IN this file (or in SKILL.md with a pointer here); side folders hold evidence, never rules; and at the start of every film the lead reads `cloud_rules/episode_lessons/` and `cloud_rules/motion/` until their content has been merged here.
- [ ] EVERY move comes from the trained motion library (templates/motion_styles), picked by action + feeling + energy + character. Always comedy. ("we did train body movement character movement you didn't use any of them here")
- [ ] Feet ON the ground, planted, never sinking or gliding. ("sometime feets is in the ground not on")
- [ ] Bodies never pass through objects. Hands END ON what they touch. Things are held, carried or pushed; nothing floats or flies in. ("treasure flying in that's also wrong")
- [ ] EXPRESSIONS: every character starts with a calm normal face. The face changes ON the narration word to fit the action or scene, never before, then returns to calm. Idle = blinks only. ("the expression made at the same time of narration, not before")
- [ ] HEAD WOBBLE: each expression change comes with a small quick head-size pop, like Rick's. ("there is no wobble like ricks")
- [ ] CHARACTER ACTING, MICRO-EXPRESSIONS, PERSONALITY-DRIVEN PHYSICAL COMEDY (CB 2026-11-13 02:03 Bangkok, pasted as a rule): characters think, feel, anticipate and react; they never just perform a mechanical action. Every significant action carries ONE motivated human behaviour detail that comes from what the character is thinking or doing, never a random add-on: tongue slightly out of one mouth corner while concentrating, one eye squinted while aiming, biting the lower lip while working, one eyebrow up when confused, head tilt while thinking, holding the breath on a delicate task. Use facial asymmetry (brows and eyes move independently), eye direction and attention shifts, reaction delays, small wrist corrections and personality body language (tense shoulders, puffed chest). Write each gag as an ACTING SEQUENCE with times: how the behaviour starts, holds and changes, e.g. drilling 0.0-1.0 s studies the target, head tilt, eyes narrow; 1.0-2.0 leans in, tongue slowly comes out without him noticing; 2.0-3.5 drills, shoulders tense, tiny wrist corrections, brows furrowed; 3.5-4.2 drill jolts, he freezes, eyes wide, tongue still out; 4.2-5.0 slow glance to the camera, tongue back in, embarrassed. Comedy comes from tiny unconscious habits, awkward pauses, overconfidence and unexpected reactions (the nervous smile and pretend-nothing-happened after a mistake; the smug half-smile while pressing the wrong button). Faces sync with the action; no frozen faces, no repeated gestures, no random expressions, no robotic moves. HOW IT FITS OUR RULES: the face still starts calm and the big change lands ON the narration word (EXPRESSIONS); the behaviour detail plays DURING the action and the acting sequence; once a character has settled, DEAD STILL IN HOLDS still wins (blinks only, no idle breathing); the head wobble comes with each expression change. The writer marks the behaviour detail per action in the shot table, the animator acts it, and the character-artist adds any face part the rig lacks (tongue-out mouth, one-eye squint, independent brows, lip bite) as a request to the lead before the shot is built.
  CB's wording (kept): "Every significant action should include a motivated human behavioral detail, where appropriate - a subtle facial habit, unconscious gesture, personality-specific reaction, or visual gag. The behavior must emerge naturally from what the character is thinking or doing, rather than being added as random animation." The goal is human-like character acting enhanced by stylized cartoon timing and physical comedy; thought-driven acting separates a character who performs an action from one who feels like a funny little human with a personality.
- [ ] UNIVERSAL VISUAL COMEDY AND GAG SYSTEM (CB 2026-11-13 02:05 Bangkok, pasted as a rule; his text kept): Automatically identify opportunities for clever, context-aware visual humor throughout every animation scene. Do not wait for the script to explicitly request a gag. Invent original visual jokes that naturally emerge from the character's goals, personality, actions, props, environment, and current story situation. PRINCIPLES: 1 Situational comedy (jokes from what is happening in the scene, not random events). 2 Visual metaphors (poverty, exhaustion, confidence, stupidity, failure or success turned into clear funny physical images). 3 Prop comedy (ordinary objects get unexpected, exaggerated or absurd behaviour that reinforces the story). 4 Character-driven humor (unconscious habits, quirks, awkward gestures, overconfidence, hesitation, exaggerated reactions; see CHARACTER ACTING). 5 Expectation reversal (set up the obvious, reveal an unexpected but understandable outcome). 6 Escalation (a small problem grows into a bigger comic consequence). 7 Physical comedy (slapstick with believable body mechanics, balance, weight and timing; BODY MECHANICS, CONTACT AND GROUNDING still apply). 8 Background comedy (occasional subtle secondary jokes that reward attention without pulling focus from the main action). 9 Silent storytelling (the gag reads without narration, dialogue or captions). 10 Comedic timing (anticipation, setup, pause, reveal, reaction, recovery; a short stillness sells the punchline). CREATIVE FREEDOM: never repeat the same joke template; choose a different gag mechanism per scene; think like an experienced cartoon storyboard artist. INTEGRATION: only where the gag adds to the scene's meaning, pacing or personality; one strong readable gag beats several weak ones; the story stays coherent, characters stay consistent, essential narration and key information are never interrupted. EXECUTION: for each gag decide setup, anticipation, visual reveal, reaction and exit transition; sell it with micro-expressions, body language, props, secondary motion and camera framing, keeping IK, limb proportions, object contact, collision, ground placement and spatial continuity. QUALITY CONTROL before finalizing: is it understood at once, does it fit this exact scene, is it visually surprising, does it reveal character or reinforce the story, is the timing readable? If not, replace it or drop it. HOW WE RUN IT: the writer proposes one gag per beat in the shot table (mechanism named, so no two scenes reuse one); the camera-director frames the reveal; the animator and vfx-artist time it; the storyboard-judge runs the five quality questions; gags stay in the story's world and period and never copy a Rick gag.
- [ ] UNIVERSAL CHARACTER PERSONALITY, PSYCHOLOGY AND SOCIAL DYNAMICS (CB 2026-11-13 02:11 Bangkok, pasted as a rule; his 13 points kept): act as a character animation director, comedy storyboard artist and performance specialist. Every character has a distinct, persistent personality that shapes how they think, move, interact, react, solve problems and behave around others. 1 PERSONALITY PROFILE: temperament, confidence, intelligence, competence, fears, motivations, emotional habits, strengths, weaknesses, quirks; kept across scenes unless the story changes them. 2 PERSONALITY-DRIVEN MOVEMENT: a calm expert moves deliberately and efficiently; a nervous beginner hesitates and overcorrects; an arrogant one exaggerates gestures; a sceptic uses restrained reactions, crossed arms, doubtful glances. 3 SHOW, DON'T TELL: personality through action, face, posture, timing, eye contact, gestures, object handling and reactions, not narration. 4 COMPETENCE AND CONFIDENCE: real skill is not the same as shown confidence (the expert works casually and precisely; the overconfident amateur performs dramatically and makes obvious mistakes). 5 SOCIAL DYNAMICS AND STATUS: how characters see and treat each other (admiration, scepticism, rivalry, disrespect, friendship, jealousy, intimidation, shifting status), shown through glances, spacing, interruptions, body language and contrasting reactions. 6 CONTRAST COMEDY: calm expert among panicking onlookers, confident fool beside a worried genius, the underestimated one who succeeds. 7 HABITS AND MICRO-EXPRESSIONS matched to the individual (see CHARACTER ACTING). 8 REACTION CHOREOGRAPHY: supporting characters are directed as carefully as the lead: true eye lines, reaction delays, facial transitions, exchanged glances, group reactions, all based on what they actually see or know. 9 EMOTIONAL CONTINUITY: emotions develop through events; no random expression changes between shots; the state and the relationships hold until the story changes them. 10 PERSONALITY GAGS from traits, relationships, unexpected competence, overconfidence, misunderstandings and clashes (see GAG SYSTEM). 11 SUBTLETY AND TIMING: not every moment is big; contrast movement and stillness; a small eyebrow raise can beat a huge cartoon reaction. 12 CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: each character keeps their posture, movement rhythm, gesture vocabulary, facial habits, reaction speed and social behaviour through the whole film. 13 VISUAL STORYTELLING: changes in relationship and status are shown in performance (the dismissed one earns respect later and is still recognisably themselves). For every scene decide what each character wants, believes, feels about the others and knows, and how their personality shapes their behaviour. Never give all characters the same generic expressions, gestures or reactions. HOW WE RUN IT: the writer writes `episodes/<name>/CAST_PERSONALITY.md` before the shot table (one profile per speaking or reacting character: the 13-point profile in short, posture, movement rhythm, 3-5 signature gestures, reaction speed, relationship to each other character, and how it changes in the story); each shot table row says what each character in frame wants, knows and feels; the animator picks library moves and timing from the profile; reactions are actions, so once a character has reacted and settled, DEAD STILL IN HOLDS applies again; the storyboard-judge fails panels where two characters react the same generic way or a reaction does not match what that character saw.
- [ ] DIALOGUE AND LIP SYNC (CB 2026-11-13 02:23 Bangkok, universal master instruction point 8): the writer finds every line of direct character speech inside the narration and marks the speaker in the shot table; narrator-only lines are marked narrator. A speaking character's mouth follows the real voice audio with phoneme-to-viseme timing (our 10 lip-sync mouths), with face, eye direction, emotion and head gestures from their personality. Characters who are not speaking never move their mouths; they listen and react (eye line to the speaker, reaction delay, then still). The narrator voice never moves a character's mouth.
- [ ] NO TELEPORT, NO MORPHING (CB 2026-11-11 on the roller coaster animatic: "many character just morph there. make rule no teleport morphing. sudden jump to a place"). A character or prop changes place ONLY by a move the viewer sees (walk, run, climb, ride, be carried, be pushed), or across a real cut or transition that the story has there. Never pop, fade, blend or slide to a new spot inside a running shot. A change of pose is ACTED through a move from the motion library (stand up, sit down, climb in, turn); never a blend from one unrelated pose into another. Things do not appear or vanish in view; they are brought in, or they are already there when the shot starts. Check: play the animatic and stop at every place change and every pose change; if you cannot name the move that got him there, it fails.

- [ ] LIGHT ON THE CHARACTERS (CB 2026-11-12: "include sunlight and light reflection, light source?"): every character is visibly lit by the scene's source. The side toward the sun, lamp, lantern or moon is brighter and takes that light's colour; a glint or rim on hair, hat, buckles and props from that source; hard shadow on the floor away from it. A card must never go dark because the light is behind it (in Blender the card takes light from both faces: diffuse + translucent, plus a small own-colour floor). Check one day and one night frame beside Rick before CB sees a set of shots.
- [ ] MICRO MOTION, THE WORLD IS NEVER FROZEN (CB 2026-11-12: "micro motions for like wind waving grass or something hit etc?"): wind sways grass, leaves, branches, curtains, cloth, hair and lantern tassels (slow, small, out of phase, never in sync); Banners and signs with words hang still and flat, so every frame can be read (CB 2026-11-13 01:51 Bangkok: "remove this rule also that makes banner move by wind"). Flags and bunting without words may still move. hanging things swing a little; anything that is hit reacts: shake, wobble, bounce, ring, dust puff, a settling sway after. Every shot names its micro motions in the shot table; a shot with nothing moving but the camera fails.
- [ ] AIR LIFE AND WEATHER (CB 2026-11-12: "dust rain snow weather etc?"): every scene has air life that fits the place: dust motes in light beams, drifting haze, steam, smoke, insects or embers; weather where the story allows it (rain, snow, falling leaves, blowing sand) with surfaces to match (wet sheen, puddles, snow on roofs) and characters reacting to it. Indoors = dust in beams, smoke from burners; night = mist and moths at lanterns.
- [ ] STUDIO-QUALITY ANIMATION, NOTHING GENERIC IN MOTION (CB 2026-11-12: "animation all high quality nothing generic. like a animation studio"): Hard Rule no. 2 applies to motion too. Every move has anticipation, the action, follow-through and overlap (head, hair, cloth and props arrive after the body), easing (slow in, slow out, never a linear tween), weight and contact (feet plant, bodies settle, hands press). DEAD STILL IN HOLDS (CB 2026-11-11 18:13Z, 'Dead still, like Rick'; measured on Rick's button press: after a move settles only the camera creeps, 0.1-0.3 px/f): once a character's move has settled, nothing on the character moves, no breathing and no sway. Blinks are allowed because they are steps. Hair, cloth and held props move only during a move and its 8-12 f settle. Wind and hit reactions stay on the WORLD (micro motion rule). Check every shot frame by frame for robotic or linear moves before CB sees it.
- [ ] LONG CLOTH MOVES WITH THE BODY (CB 2026-11-12 19:30 Bangkok "ok"): in every library move (pose m:<id> in films, rig_cast in tests) a long cloth (S.skirt) and a cape (S.behind) follow the legs the motion rig draws: upright the hem follows the legs; sitting it lies over the lap; kneeling, crouching, crawling or lying it wraps the legs and stops at the floor, never through a seat or the ground. No long bare legs beside a stiff robe. Cloth swings only during a move and settles within 8 to 12 frames; in a hold it is dead still. Keep it simple like Rick's robes. Check any new long outfit in walk, run, sit, kneel, jump, crawl and fall on the three body sizes before CB sees it.

- [ ] MOTION BLUR AND SPEED LINES (CB 2026-11-12 01:09 Bangkok: "no blur on character", speed lines "can have but make them look premium not like a kids cartoon"): characters are NEVER motion-blurred (a new sharp pose every frame, as Rick); fast moves get 1-2 smear frames instead. Motion blur is allowed on the world and fast props only (wheels, thrown things, the background in a whip). Speed lines are allowed again (this replaces the 2026-11-10 "no speed lines" line in the kit) but premium: thin, tapered, few, soft glow or air-streak in the scene's light colour, short-lived, following the real direction of travel; never thick black comic lines, stars or clip-art bursts.
- [ ] SATISFYING VFX AND HIGHLIGHTS (CB 2026-11-12: "visual effects, highlights must feel satisfying"): every effect lands ON the beat with build, pop and settle: a short wind-up, a hit frame (squash, flash of glow, bloom, sparks or particles, ink splash, a 2-4 frame camera shake on big hits), then a settle (sparkles fade, dust drifts down, the object wobbles to rest). Clean readable shapes in the story colours, sized to be seen at phone size, always with a matching SFX. Never a weak flat overlay, a plain fade-in or a static sticker. Check each effect at full speed AND frame by frame.
- [ ] REAL-WORLD PHYSICS, BODY ANGLE MATCHES THE CAMERA (CB 2026-11-12: "real world physis, camera angle body angle"): things have weight. They fall with gravity, swing and settle, bounce less each time, slide and stop with friction, and carry momentum through a move; nothing floats or stops dead. Each character's view (front, 3/4, side, back), feet and perspective agree with where the camera is: a low camera sees him from below (bigger feet, smaller head, chin up), (no high or top-down camera on a character: see FULL BODY FORM below), a camera to his side sees his side. Check: for every card, name the camera position and the view it must show.
- [ ] FULL BODY FORM, NEVER SQUASH: THE CAMERA COMES DOWN TO THE CHARACTER (CB 2026-11-12 10:44Z: "always show charcter the full form. neverr sqash. The full bodyform. need follow camera angle"; 11:05Z, rejecting the card-tilt method: "We study so many ricks clips. Please take the rules from there. Camera never stands at that angle need to pan down to the form of character"; measured on Rick's cart army, pink prison, grave bell, knight, drivers). Whenever a character is in frame, the camera stands at the character's height: between chest and eye level for talk and acts, or low near the ground looking up for power. Down-angle from camera to the character's chest at most 10 degrees. Characters always stand upright (card turns only around the vertical axis, Blender LOCKED_TRACK lock Z); never tip the card toward the lens. High or top-down views are only for objects and places with no character in frame. If a shot starts high on the set, the camera cranes/pans DOWN to the character's height before or as the character enters. Check: compute the down-angle to every character per shot before rendering. (Magic bell: anim_hook AN "crane" {cam, aim, end}. The TRACK_TO card tilt is withdrawn.)
- [ ] CHARACTER TRAITS MATCH THE STORY + CARTOON POWER VFX (CB 2026-11-12: "character eigenschaften match the story. use cartoon vfx or super power effects"): each character's look, outfit, build, props and way of moving say their role at first sight (clever judge = calm, tidy, sly half-smile; guilty thief = shifty eyes, sweat, hunched; brave guard = puffed chest). Feelings and acts are shown with cartoon effects in the story colours: sweat drops, anger steam, blush, a sparkle on a clever idea, a guilt aura or dark cloud, speed lines, shock lines, glowing eyes, stars after a hit, a power glow on the hero object. Every main beat gets at least one, on the narration word, built, popped and settled like the other VFX.
- [ ] HANDS ON OBJECTS, MARCHING CROWDS, GRASS (CB 2026-11-12, cart army lessons, LESSONS_FOR_FUTURE.md): hands end on the object; for a 3D tool draw 3D arms from the card shoulder to named points on the tool with a round fist (ep_arms + noArms pose, tube = 19 px limb line); bearers stand at pole ends with a fist on the pole at shoulder height; spear fists on the shaft, other hand behind the shield. A marching crowd uses four walk frames per soldier on its own phase, with a high knee lift so it reads from the front. Grass moves in the wind (vertex shader waves).
- [ ] BODY MECHANICS, CONTACT AND GROUNDING (CB 2026-11-13 02:01 Bangkok: "aplly this rule"; his full list: anatomically plausible posing, contact-aware animation, IK, joint constraints, physically believable object interaction, no floating, no ground penetration). For our 2D vector puppets in the three.js kit and in Blender: (1) FIXED LIMB LENGTHS: arms and legs keep their rig length (the 19 px limb line) in every pose; never stretch a limb to reach. (2) IK, NOT LOOSE LIMBS: a hand or foot goes to a target point and the arm or leg is solved from the shoulder or hip with a two-bone bend at fixed lengths (ep_arms / grips.mjs for hands); if the target is out of reach, the body moves, turns or bends first (body-driven motion). (3) JOINT LIMITS: elbows and knees bend only the natural way, wrists and ankles within a natural range; no reversed knee, no broken elbow, no disconnected limb. (4) HANDS LOCKED ON OBJECTS: the centre of the round fist sits on the named grip point and stays locked there while held; the object follows the hand with no sliding, floating, drifting or clipping; reach, grip, lift, carry, set down, release are separate acted steps (approach with feet set, bend hips and knees, both hands on the grip points, lift with legs and body, carry stable, lower onto a surface before letting go). (5) WEIGHT: every move starts from the body with anticipation and follow-through; hips and feet shift when lifting, pushing, pulling or turning; the centre of gravity stays over the feet unless the character is falling; limbs move on arcs, no robotic straight interpolation and no needless limb motion. (6) FEET PLANTED: in a stance phase the foot's world position does not move (no foot sliding); walks use foot locking per step; standing characters have both weight-bearing feet on the ground. (7) GROUNDING: feet snap to the real ground height at their position (raycast to the terrain in three.js, the same positions in Blender from the lock); no hovering above, no sinking into floors, stairs, grass or furniture; a seated character touches the seat; every still prop rests on a support surface; unsupported things fall. (8) NO CLIPPING: bodies, limbs and props never pass through walls, furniture, other characters or each other (see PHYSICAL BODIES). (9) SPATIAL CONSISTENCY: scale, depth, height and world position stay consistent from frame to frame; no teleporting (NO TELEPORT). (10) FRAME CHECK BEFORE RENDER: before any render, check dense frames (every contact, every step, every grip and release, and every 0.5 s) for floating, ground penetration, clipping, foot sliding, missing support and broken contact; contact shadows (CONTACT SHADOW) go under feet and props, but they never hide a real gap. Cartoon exaggeration of anticipation and impact is welcome; contact points, ground placement and object hold stay physically right.
  CB's wording, BODY POSITION & LIMB INTERACTION RULES: All character animations must use anatomically plausible posing, correct joint articulation, inverse kinematics (IK), realistic weight distribution, and contact-aware object interaction. Maintain consistent limb lengths and natural shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, and ankle positions. Never allow impossible joint rotations, disconnected limbs, body intersections, or unnatural stretching. When reaching for or grabbing an object, position the entire arm using IK, rotate the wrist toward the contact point, and establish precise hand-to-object contact. Lock the gripping hand to the object while held. The object must follow the hand without sliding, floating, or clipping. All movements must originate from the body and respect balance, center of gravity, momentum, anticipation, and follow-through. Shift the hips and feet appropriately when lifting, pushing, pulling, turning, or changing direction. Use grounded feet with no foot sliding, believable contact and release transitions, and physically coherent timing. Avoid robotic interpolation, unnecessary limb movement, and excessive smoothing. Every action must have a clear intention and readable silhouette.
  CB's wording, GROUNDING, COLLISION & ANTI-FLOATING RULES: All characters, props, and environmental objects must maintain physically consistent positions in 3D space. 1 NO FLOATING (never hover above the ground or a support unless jumping, flying or suspended on purpose). 2 NO GROUND PENETRATION (feet, legs, objects and body parts never sink into or pass through floors, walls, furniture or other solid geometry). 3 FOOT GROUNDING (foot IK, ground detection, planted-foot constraints, terrain alignment; feet stay on the ground in stance without sliding). 4 OBJECT GROUNDING (every still object rests on a valid support surface). 5 COLLISION AWARENESS (no unintended intersections between characters, limbs, props and the set). 6 ACCURATE CONTACT POINTS (hands to objects, feet to the ground, seated characters to chairs). 7 SPATIAL CONSISTENCY (scale, depth, elevation, distance and world position stay right in every frame). 8 GRAVITY AND WEIGHT (unsupported objects fall unless a force or constraint holds them). 9 STABLE INTERACTION (held objects stay anchored to the right hand positions; no drifting, teleporting or detaching). 10 FRAME-BY-FRAME VALIDATION (check floating, ground penetration, clipping, foot sliding, missing support and broken contact before rendering). In Blender and three.js use raycasting for ground detection and collision-aware IK for feet; standing characters lock their weight-bearing feet to valid ground; contact shadows under characters and objects. Final: every character, limb, prop and environment object obeys consistent spatial relationships, grounded contact, collision constraints, gravity and believable weight; no unintended floating, ground penetration, clipping, sliding or disconnected interaction in any frame.
  CB's wording, STYLIZED 2.5D STICKMAN CHARACTERS (our vector puppets): Fixed limb lengths: never stretch stick arms or legs to reach an object. Contact anchors: the centre of each dot hand aligns with the intended grip location. Body-driven motion: rotate or reposition the torso when an object is outside comfortable arm reach. Strong silhouettes: keep arms and hands visually separated from the torso when possible. Stylized weight: exaggerated anticipation and impact, but believable contact and balance. Treat hands, feet and objects as physically connected during contact; all poses are solved through body mechanics and IK, not by moving limbs independently.
- [ ] NO FLICKERING FLOOR, NO SLIDING WALK, NO BODY INSIDE FURNITURE (CB 2026-11-15 on the goldrush final v2: "0.11 floor is flicker, the seller also sliding insted of walking. also his body is in the table", "0.32 at the river 0.54 floor flickering", "0.59 the miner is in the table", "the women have shade on her face and also is in the table. please avpoid these"). (1) FLOOR AND GROUND NEVER FLICKER: shadows, light patches and textures on floors, decks and ground stay stable from frame to frame while the camera moves (no shadow-map shimmer, no lamp flicker that jumps the whole floor); a lamp may flicker only as a small, slow change on what it lights. Measured on the rendered frames before CB sees them (flicker scan of the floor region: frame-to-frame change no bigger than the camera's own move explains). (2) A WALK IS A WALK: a character who changes place walks with planted feet whose stride matches the distance travelled (motion library walk, foot locked per step); never a card gliding while the legs cycle or stand. (3) NO BODY INSIDE FURNITURE: counters, tables, chairs and tubs are solid: a character stands or sits BESIDE or BEHIND them with the whole body on the right side of the surface, seen from the camera; a seated character's legs go under a table only where the table is open. Checked per rest by the frame checker (body and head inside a set mesh) and by eye on a zoom sheet. (4) FACES CLEAN: no shadow, shade band or dark patch on a face from a table, hat, prop or light (extends NO HAT OR HAIR BRIM SHADOW ON FACES).

## 10. THE PROVEN BUILD METHOD (pin stretch test, CB 2026-11-14: "Yes, rebuild film". Proof: episodes/armor-no-holes/stretches/armor-pins-test)
- A film is built in STRETCHES of one place each (10-25 s), one builder per stretch for the build, and a FRESH builder for every fix round who starts from the stretch's STATE.md (section 11, T2; changed 2026-11-15 because a builder kept for 13 hours cost 184 million tokens). Each stretch is ONE continuous take: the camera flies, lands, rests, flies again; no cut inside a stretch. Stretches join only where the place changes, through an object or a 8-12 frame blend.
- Every act of every character is an episode move written for that act (a moves file in the stretch's cast folder, loaded as `m:../../<file>/<style>`), drawn new on every frame: `tween.ones` true, `face_frames` 0. Count before any render: plain kit poses 0, frozen moves 0.
- Things that go in, on or at something FLY there and HIT: flight with a streak, a one-frame hit, a mark, a quiver, dust, and the thing that is hit shudders. Nothing just appears.
- Act frames are plain frame numbers taken from words.json, never shifted by a tool.
- Sheets made for every render and looked at by the builder AND the lead before CB: a strip at 4 frames per second, the LINE CHECK (each line's words beside its frames: do I see what it says?), feet and eyes zooms, a phone-size sheet.
- Still owed after the test, check on every stretch: nobody cut by the frame edge at any frame of a rest; floor at most a third of a wide; the small story thing (a pin, a chip, a chalk ring) large enough to read on a phone at the moment its word is said; props in hands as real 3D props where the kit can.
- Renders: full-size frames in parallel chunks (`episodes/armor-no-holes/stretches/armor-pins-test/render_final.sh` is the pattern). With several builders on one PC, at most 3 render processes per builder.
- CLOSE-UPS ON WHAT THE VOICE NAMES, AS A SECONDARY RULE THAT MUST MATCH THE SCENE (CB 2026-11-14 on the joined armor film: "there are some like close up missing and frame by narration", "When you say hole, you need to show a hole", "Zoom to a hole"; then, correcting the lead who made it the top rule: "It's not primary, it's secondary. It needs to match the scene."). The scene comes first: its staging, its acting, the flow of the take. Where it fits that scene, the camera flies in and lands close on the thing the voice names, on the word, rests a beat and flies on; a named part may be highlighted with an effect. Never force a close-up on every noun and never chop a take into a string of inserts.
- NOBODY CUT IN HALF, STANCES PHYSICALLY RIGHT (CB same day: "at second 9, he had removed by half", "when he stands on the ladder, it's like a wrong position"). Check every frame of a rest for a figure cut by the frame edge; anyone on a ladder, box or step has both soles on a visible tread and the body on the right side of it. Zoom on it before sending.
- HOW RICK DOES IT, MEASURED (4 films, 106 named things; study `episodes/armor-no-holes/refs/closeup_study/CLOSEUP_STUDY.md`, 2026-11-14): 96 % of named things are shown on their word, about 40 % close, 57 % in the scene view. A close-up is a push inside the running take (0.3-0.5 s in), the thing DOES something for about 1 s, then the camera pulls back or tilts to a face; a hand, tool or face is in it, light and place match the wide, the action never stops. A part is highlighted with the part itself (glow or colour running along it, glint, dust, a real marker); no outlines, arrows or floating labels, and the rest is not dimmed without a real cause. "Many of one thing" is revealed in under half a second with a hand placing the newest.
- RENDER ON THE GRAPHICS CARD (CB 2026-11-14: "Can you not use gpu all work?"). `templates/threejs_film/render_gpu.mjs` draws the three.js frames on the RTX 2070 SUPER: about 0.55-0.9 s per full-size frame against 4.7 s in software, picture equal apart from antialiased edges (tested on one film; `GPU_RENDER.md`). One process normally, two only when the card is free, never three, never while Blender uses the card. Never mix software and GPU frames inside one stretch. Check one frame per place both ways before a full run. Why the first try was black: a `pow()` of a slightly negative number in a set shader gives not-a-number on the card, and the bloom blur spread it; any new set shader must guard `pow`, `sqrt` and divisions.
- BLENDER LAYERS ON RUNPOD (CB 2026-11-14: "ok do runpod"). Blender layer frames render on rented RTX 4090 machines, not on our card: the picture matches local to 0.005 of 255, so cloud and local frames can share a shot. One Blender process is held up by the processor (tens of thousands of objects set per frame), so the speed comes from 6-8 processes per machine (4.2-4.6 s a frame against 23 s here) and from several machines at once. Steps and image in `episodes/armor-no-holes/blender_metal/RUNPOD.md` (needs `libegl1 libgl1 libopengl0`). Only the lead creates machines; check a machine's upload speed in the first 2 minutes and drop a slow one (one upload crawled at 18 MB in 20 minutes); terminate each machine the moment its frames are counted on this PC. Armor film: 362 metal frames, about 1 h 20 min of machine time, about 1.30 USD. Put the Blender layer only where the thing it improves covers at least 1.5 % of the picture (measured per frame on the matte); in wide shots it adds glints and nothing to see.

## RULES FROM OTHER SECTIONS THAT NAME YOUR SUBJECT
### from 0. How to work (before anything is built)
- [ ] Load this file, SKILL.md (THE PIPELINE, movement rule, MAIN LOOK, 3D WORLD STYLE) and HANDOFF.md from the PC skill at the start of every session. Notes and memory are not the skill. ("it install in the skill. and everytime you should check the skill")

### from 3. World and look (Rick's 3D world, never a flat drawing)
- [ ] FEET SEEN ON THE FLOOR (CB 2026-11-11: "our chracters we dont see the feet. is like in the floor somehow"): soles sit on the TOP of the floor surface (check the floor height), with a shadow, and no prop in front of the feet.
- [ ] WORDS IN THE WORLD ARE ALLOWED, like Rick's (CB 2026-11-11, roller coaster thread: "remove the no text rule"). Banners, signs, shop fronts, cart names and labels carry short readable words that tell the story at a glance ("GRAND OPENING TOMORROW", "FIRST!"). Bold hand-painted lettering, 1-4 words, spelled right, readable at phone size. The old "no readable text anywhere" rule is gone. (Faces with drawn text stay out: section 4.)
- [ ] RICK CAMERA AND SET BUILD (CB 2026-11-11: "did you learn also about camera movement and angle and environment overhaul, sets build"; measured frame by frame on his roller coaster film against our animatic of the same shots):
  - The camera almost never stops: he moves on 88 % of frames with about 1 rest per 10 s; ours moved on 55 % with 5 rests per 10 s. Plan ONE slow continuous move per beat (median 1.6 s, up to 6-10 s), not fast hops between stations: his moving speed is half ours.
  - Push in a little all the time (54 % of his frames), pull back for a reveal (23 %), tilt up or down a tall thing with the action. A whip only at a scene change.
  - Angles tell the story: on the ground looking up (hammer, loop, car), high looking down (cart over the hill), over the cart nose (POV), a tipped horizon in danger beats. Eye level only for talk.
  - Something big and close in every frame: track bed, roof beam, cart nose, post, sign.
  - The subject comes to the lens (car, cart) instead of the camera jumping to it.
  - ONE connected world: every day shot looks into the same valley from another side (same Ferris wheel, track, fields, hills), not separate little sets.
  - Twice our detail (edge density 0.087 vs 0.047, colours per frame 17 vs 13): structures built from real parts (cross bracing, ladders, ties, separate boards), tree lines and clumps instead of single round trees on a grid, fenced fields, paths, worn dirt where things stand, small far buildings and people.
  - Structures tower over people (tiny figure, huge loop), then very close on the face or hands.
  - Deep blue sky with a few small clouds; dark roofs and shadow areas next to bright sunlit ground, not every surface bright.
- [ ] THE CODED FRAME HAS REAL METAL, REAL SURFACE RELIEF AND A REAL SKY (CB 2026-11-15 on lightning spear final v1: "quality can be much better. more details. iron speeer need metallic detail and the sky looks weired", "gold angle more detailed. stomr bell made metallic gold. even the floor looks to vector with no textuire. the trees also, the bell wheel also", "what cause that you dindt make it right in the beginning?"). WHY IT HAPPENED: every set used the kit's flat 3-step toon material (no metal can shine in it), surface textures were flat colour pictures with no relief, the sky was a gradient with flat cloud blobs, trees were simple clumps, and the lead judged detail on 135-360 px sheets without a side-by-side with Rick; the armor film's metal had come from a Blender layer, which the lean pipeline switched off. RULE: (1) metal, gold, bronze, glass and wet things use the kit's PBR path (physical material with an environment map from the scene's own sky, brushed or hammered normal map, clearcoat on gilt), never the toon material; (2) stone, brick, tile, wood, cobbles, mud and bark carry a normal or bump map plus colour variation, never a flat painted picture; (3) the sky has volume (layered lit clouds with soft edges and depth), per light kind; (4) trees have trunks with bark, branch forks and many leaf clusters with light and shade; (5) every hero object the voice names (here: spear, bracket, wire, bell, bell wheel, gold angel) is a detailed model with at least 10 named parts, made FIRST, alone, and checked full size beside a Rick hero object before any stretch uses it; (6) the LEAD looks at 8 random frames per stretch at full width (at least 540 px wide each) beside Rick frames before CB sees a version: small sheets are only for staging.

### from 4. Characters
- [ ] FACE SHADOW: THE DRAWN ONE STAYS, THE GENERATED ONE NEVER (CB 2026-11-15 on lightning spear final v1: "still have shadow on his face. we had a rule to remove it", then, when the lead removed the drawn one too: "dont delete this premade face shadow. the wone that generate shadow on face only"). The template's own drawn face shadow (char2d faceShadow) STAYS on every character (film.json face_shadow true or unset). What is removed is every GENERATED shade on a face: the kit's card_shade (amount 0 AND rim_amount 0), the far light, any scene or costume shade on skin. Confirms FACE SHADE: ONLY THE DRAWN ONE below. The kit bug that ignored a sheet's faceShadow is fixed (castkit + puppets.mjs, film.json key face_shadow). Second generated shade found the same day (CB: "there is still generated shadow on the mud scene. on the chracter face and chicken"): costume_shade treated the outer drawn crescent and a white animal's body as costume and darkened them in a hard ramp; every film sets `costume_shade.keep_drawn_light: true` (kit film.js, default off for old films), which leaves every white and light-grey drawn pixel exactly as drawn.
- [ ] FACE SHADE: ONLY THE DRAWN ONE (CB 2026-11-13 night: "No shade on faces. keep the drawn shade that make 3d look. but no shade from hair or hat or anything else on face."). The soft shade the character template itself draws on the face, which makes the head read as a 3D form, STAYS. Nothing else may put shade on a face: no shadow from hair, hat or brim, no costume shade on skin, no shadow cast by a prop, an arm or another character, no card light or scene light that darkens the face in patches. Where older lines differ (RICK EDGE SHADOW, the night line "the face goes darker with the scene"), this line wins: the face may take the COLOUR of the scene light, but only the template's own shade shapes it. Check on every sheet with the eyes zoom: a grey patch on a face that the template did not draw = fix before sending.
- [ ] NO COLOURED LIGHT RIM ON A FACE, NO HORIZONTAL STREAKS IN HAIR (CB 2026-11-15, lightning spear hook frame: "please remove the lines at his hair and also the orange light on his face", then "not the curl. the horizontal lines"). (1) The kit's card rim (card_shade rim_amount with the sun colour, and the `far` light) painted an orange band on the hero's cheek at dusk. Faces stay clean white with only the template's own soft shade: set `card_shade.amount` 0 AND `card_shade.rim_amount` 0 and no `far` colour light for the cast in every place (CB 2026-11-15 again, on the hook clip: "why keep making the same mistake? the shadow on his face": with rim 0 the kit's card_shade still painted a grey band on the far side of the face at amount 0.55; only the template's own thin crescent may shade a face); the warm light is shown on the costume, the props and the set. (2) The costume shade measured its ramp per pixel row, so hair beside the white face showed horizontal streaks. ### from 6. Camera, transitions, effects, sound
- [ ] CAMERA: FLY, LAND, REST, FLY AGAIN (CB 2026-11-13 evening on the bomber armor animatic: "the camera movement is not what rick clips do", "too many cuts and just short camera fly, ricks clips have longer camere fly and stop then move. our move constant but in small moves only"; measured the same night on his roller coaster, cart army and railroads films against our animatic with one tracker, study in episodes/armor-no-holes/refs/camera_study/CAMERA_STUDY.md). This REPLACES every older line that says the camera never stops or moves 88-100 % of the time (CAMERA MOVEMENT ALWAYS, RICK CAMERA AND SET BUILD, the film check's rest and speed bands): measured with the film check's own line he RESTS 20-29 % of the time. His rhythm: a flight, a landing, a rest in which the picture itself changes (acting, an effect, a board filling), then the next flight. Numbers to hit: 2-3 LONG flights of 3 s or more per film (his longest 4.7-9.4 s), each attached to a moving thing or a line in the set; 21-45 % of the film inside flights of 2 s or more (ours 13 %); slow creep at most about 20 % (ours 39 %); the first flight starts inside the first second (ours 4.1 s); shot changes are 0.3 s dissolves with the camera moving through them, 12-13 a minute, and hard cuts 1-5 a minute, none in the first 20 s (ours 14 hard, 0 dissolves). Go from place to place by FLYING through the connected set where it allows it, and blend only where the clock jumps. CB's own words on it the same night: "camere stops often. but i think it mean is mostly constaty moing not cuting frame if is not ncessary only when it change to another different location. also transition in object thats introduce a new scenen is is alos good to have." So: the camera stops often, and that is right; what "always moving" means is ONE continuous camera that flies and rests without cutting the frame; a cut or blend comes only when the story goes to a different location; and a transition THROUGH AN OBJECT that introduces the new scene (the next place first seen inside a thing in the present shot, the camera goes into it) is wanted at those changes. TOOLS TO CORRECT before the next camera plan: the film check bands (rest share, speed median, travel p90 as a hard gate, no ban on flights over 7 s), the plan gate that forces a stop on every named word, a hook gate (first flight inside 1 s), and the kit must draw planned blends as dissolves, not cuts.
- [ ] Shot size follows the story: wide for places and group beats, close for lines, reactions, hands and hero objects, medium for the rest. ("camera need to match story some wide some closed")
- [ ] Real viewpoints with depth: low and close, POV, over the shoulder; a new angle each shot. Faces above the caption line. Wides: characters at least a third of frame height, floor at most a third. No back view of the subject.
- [ ] Key actions get a push-in to the hand and object with a light on it. ("zoom to the hand and bell, light pointing")
- [ ] FOLLOW THE REFERENCE CAMERA MOVE, NOT ONLY ITS STILLS (CB 2026-11-11: "make a comparison didt you follow the camera movement?"). Matching frames at fixed seconds is not a camera match. Measured on the roller coaster match: his camera moving 87 % of the time, ours 59 %; 30 of 64 seconds had a different move; he has ONE hard cut in 63 s, ours showed about ten jumps. For a match film, or any shot built from a Rick reference: track his move per second (push in, pull back, pan, tilt, speed; script: track features between frames, caption band masked) and build ours to the same move, start frame, end frame and speed; cut only where he cuts; use his transition kind (dissolve, whip, ride-through). Before CB sees an animatic, make the side-by-side video (his left, ours right, his sound) and watch it yourself.
- [ ] CAMERA MOVEMENT, ALWAYS (CB 2026-11-12 20:49 Bangkok, cart army thread: "always remember the camera movement"; measured table in project files episodes/cart-army/LESSONS_FOR_FUTURE.md): measured on Rick's cart army film the camera moves 100 % of the time; 6 hard cuts in 67 s and none before 39 s; push in 69 %, pull back 12 %; his opening moves are half our speed. Every picture has one slow continuous move. Join pictures with the move itself (whip, ride over, orbit) or a 6-14 frame blend, hard cuts only for a late shock beat. Pull back to reveal about one move in eight. With a character in frame the camera stays at character height, at most 10 degrees down (see FULL BODY FORM). Measure ours against his with the tracker in a side-by-side before CB sees it.

- [ ] HIGH-QUALITY VFX AND CAMERA WITH A PURPOSE (CB 2026-11-13 02:23 Bangkok, universal master instruction points 6 and 9; the cart army 36-shot review found white spaghetti trails, flat orange circles and wheels shown instead of the loaded launcher). Effects are layered and follow the motion, never placeholders: PROJECTILES are real meshes on separate, believable flight paths with depth and perspective, trails aligned to velocity; SMOKE has plume shape, turbulence, soft see-through edges, density changes, a direction and fades out naturally, trails taper; EXPLOSIONS and IMPACTS = bright first flash, then expanding smoke, dust, sparks and debris, light thrown on the surroundings, and a fading trail; PARTICLES have a real emission point, speed, lifetime, drag and size variation; LIGHT EFFECTS are emissive with controlled glow and real reflected light. Camera response (small shake, focus change, impact framing) only when the action earns it. Motion blur on world, props and projectiles only, never on characters. Never random white curves, big flat circles or disconnected glowing shapes. CAMERA: CAMERA MOVEMENT, ALWAYS still holds (the camera never stops), and every move also has a story purpose: the framing shows what the sentence is about (a close-up when an object or action must be understood, never a wide instead; the event dominates the frame, e.g. the blast, not the wall). Keep screen direction, object positions and character relationships across cuts; no accidental cropping, repeated identical moves or wide empty space.



### from 6b. RICK REFERENCE LESSONS (2026-11-11, thread "Learn from Rick's Clips reference videos";
- [ ] CAMERA TRAVELS MORE: his picture moves about twice as far per second as ours. Lens down in the grass with big blades in front, push in on the hero object, follow a moving thing (spark down a rope, rockets into the sky).
- [ ] ENDING: the last beat is the hero's punchline face (smug, arms crossed) in front of the result.
- [ ] FOUR PASSES ON TOP OF THE PLAIN BUILD (CB's source, checked on the cart film): 1 camera (close, one face can fill the screen; camera-director), 2 environment (real textured sets; Stage 1/2 + real models), 3 POST ON THE WORLD ONLY: render the cast as its own layer, put fog, haze, depth of field, bloom and grade on the world, then lay the cast on top (light grade on the cast only), so characters are never blurred or fogged; 4 SHADING: a pale light streak along the lit edge of face and clothes (inner rim, head and body, not a frame around hats), the existing soft shadow on the far side, and a SHADOW PASS: a hidden copy of each card turned to face the sun casts the shadow, so the shadow is a full figure, never a thin sliver when the sun is to the side.

### from 8. Build fixes learned (magic bell, 2026-11-11). Each one cost a re-render; check them bef
- [ ] Run `proj.py tune.json` before EVERY render: each card's feet and head must land inside 0.08..0.92 of the frame width, and the camera must not sit inside any set object (booth radius, candle stands, walls). A camera inside geometry gives a black or curtain-only frame.
- [ ] Group rows: space cards so raised hands do not cover a neighbour's face (about 0.95 m apart for arms-up poses, wider lens), and check no face is cut by the frame edge.
- [ ] Hands on an object: cards turn toward the camera, so place the card origin at hand point minus the hand offset (from cards/meta.json) along screen-right, with the hand a few cm in front of the surface facing the camera; otherwise the hand sinks behind the object.
- [ ] Held props are drawn AT the hand in the card (P.held svg): palms, ink brush, chest, cookie. Never a separate floating prop.
- [ ] Props that prove the story are built in 3D with their marks: the ink bell = glossy black body, four bronze handprints wiped out of the ink (palm + 4 fingers + thumb), drips at the lip.
- [ ] Dark limbs vanish on dark objects (ink-black arm on the black ink bell): draw a white open palm at the hand (cards_gen over.palmHand) so every touch reads. Place a touch card WITHOUT the mirror flag (mirror puts the hand on the other side).
- [ ] Card lighting in Blender (2026-11-12): the card shader takes light from both faces (diffuse + translucent) with an own-colour floor of 0.7 by day and 0.35 at night, plus a key-side band: the half toward the key is brighter in the key colour, the far half takes a cool shadow tint (hall_head.py card(), tune card_emit, card_side, card_band). Do not stack edge_shadow.py on v12+ cards: the template draws the face shadow.
